questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state the assumption a linear calibration rests on
questions.stem: A calibration curve is built by plotting instrument response against known analyte concentration. What assumption does the straight-line section of that curve rest on?

options.text: response stays proportional to concentration across the plotted range, so an unknown can be interpolated
response rises to a fixed maximum once the analyte is fully ionised and stays there
options.misconception: believes a detector saturates at a fixed maximum signal

options.text: the slope is unchanged at every concentration the instrument can ever reach
options.misconception: extends the linear range to the whole capacity of the instrument

options.text: each standard is measured in a different solvent from the unknown samples
options.misconception: insists standards and unknowns must sit in different matrices

questions.explanation: A straight line on a response against concentration plot is the statement that response is proportional to concentration, and that proportionality is what lets an unknown reading be read off the line by interpolation. The trap is treating linearity as a property of the instrument everywhere; it holds only over the range actually covered by standards, and outside that range a fitted line is an extrapolation with no evidence behind it. The solvent condition is not part of the assumption, though matching the matrix between standards and samples is good practice for a different reason.
questions.hint: Ask what the gradient of the plotted line means physically.

questions.learningObjective: correct a reading for the blank and justify the sign
questions.stem: A spectrophotometer reads 0.845 for a sample and 0.112 for a blank that contains everything in the sample except the analyte. What corrected absorbance follows, and why?

options.misconception: adds the blank to the sample, treating background as analyte

options.text: 0.112, because only the blank signal is due to the analyte of interest
options.misconception: treats the blank reading as the analyte response

options.text: 7.54, because the sample reading is divided by the blank reading
options.misconception: divides by the blank instead of subtracting it

Subtraction rather than addition is forced by the logic of what the blank represents. A blank is not background noise to be averaged in; it is a measurement of the apparatus and reagents, and keeping any of it in the reported value inflates the result, while adding it inflates the result twice over.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish equivalence, neutrality and end point in a titration
questions.stem: In an acid base titration the moles of added titrant become equal to the moles of analyte present. What does that equality mark?

options.text: the equivalence point, where the ratio required by the balanced equation is exactly met
the neutral point, where the pH is exactly 7 whatever the reagents involved
options.misconception: confuses equivalence with neutrality, which coincide only for a strong acid against a strong base

options.text: the end point, which the analyst may choose freely before the titration is begun
options.misconception: believes the end point is a matter of analyst preference rather than chemistry

options.text: the saturation point, beyond which no further titrant can dissolve in the mixture
options.misconception: reads a reagent endpoint as a solubility limit

The end point is a measurement of the equivalence point and is a good one only when it falls on the steep part of the curve.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement is about moles, about pH, or about a signal.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: name and define the two phases every separation requires
questions.stem: Every form of chromatography requires two phases. What are they?

options.text: a mobile phase that carries the sample and a stationary phase it travels along or against
a gas phase and a liquid phase, both of which must be present in every separation

options.text: a solid support and a porous membrane of identical chemical composition
options.misconception: imagines the two phases must be made of the same material

What the two phases must differ in is their ability to interact with the analytes, not their physical state.

questions.topic: Concentration of a calibration standard by dilution

questions.stem: A 5.00 mL aliquot of a 0.400 mol/L stock solution is diluted to a final volume of 25.00 mL. What molarity, in mol/L, does the calibration standard have? Report the number only.

The trap is reading 25 mL as 250 mL, which would make the standard ten times too dilute, and the other trap is dividing by the aliquot instead of the final volume, which inverts the whole operation. questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute an absorbance from absorptivity, concentration and path length
questions.stem: A solution has a molar absorptivity of 1.20e3 L mol-1 cm-1, a concentration of 5.00e-4 mol/L and a cell path length of 1.00 cm. What absorbance does it show? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The Beer-Lambert law states that absorbance equals the absorptivity times the concentration times the path length, so 1.20e3 times 5.00e-4 times 1.00 is 0.600. Back-substituting by rearranging to a concentration and multiplying by the same path length returns 0.600, which confirms the product has been assembled in the right order. Forgetting the path length gives 0.600 only by luck here because the cell is 1.00 cm, which is exactly why a 1 cm cell is the usual default.
questions.hint: Multiply the three quantities in the order the law names them.

questions.stem: On a thin layer chromatography plate the solvent front travelled 9.00 cm from the origin and a spot travelled 4.50 cm from the same origin. What retardation factor did that spot have? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The retardation factor is the distance moved by the compound divided by the distance moved by the solvent front, both measured from the origin, so 4.50 cm over 9.00 cm is 0.500. questions.topic: Chemical shift from a frequency offset
questions.learningObjective: convert a frequency offset into a chemical shift
questions.stem: A proton resonance in a 300 MHz spectrometer lies 240 Hz downfield of the reference. What chemical shift, in parts per million, is that? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Chemical shift in parts per million is the frequency offset divided by the operating frequency, so 240 Hz over 300 MHz is 0.800 ppm. Expressing the operating frequency in hertz instead gives 240 divided by 3.00e8 Hz, and multiplying by 1e6 to return to parts per million gives the same 0.800, so the units are consistent either way. The reason the shift is quoted in parts per million is that the offset in hertz scales with field strength, while the shift in ppm does not.

questions.learningObjective: obtain a mass to charge value from an ion mass and its charge
questions.stem: A neutral molecule has a molar mass of 64.1 g/mol. At what mass to charge value does its singly charged molecular ion appear in a mass spectrum? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The mass to charge value of an ion is its mass divided by the number of charges it carries, so a single charge leaves the value equal to the mass, 64.1. A doubly charged ion of the same mass would appear near 32.1, which is why multiply charged species appear at lower mass to charge values than their neutral masses would suggest. The molecular ion is the intact molecule after loss of an electron, so its mass is that of the molecule less one electron, a difference far below the resolution of the instrument.

questions.learningObjective: compute a peak resolution and interpret it as a pure number
questions.stem: Two peaks are recorded at retention times 4.20 and 4.68 min with base widths of 0.30 and 0.30 min. What resolution does the resolution expression give, and how should it be read?

0.48 min, which is the time gap between the two peak maxima
options.misconception: reports the numerator of the expression and keeps it in time units

options.text: 0.625, which comes from dividing the average peak width by the gap
options.misconception: inverts the resolution expression so a wider pair scores better

options.text: 9.75, which comes from dividing the later retention time by the gap

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why one mass spectrum is not a structure
questions.learningObjective: explain the limits of a single mass spectrum for structure assignment
questions.stem: Explain why one clean mass spectrum, even with a clear molecular ion, is not enough to assign a structure, and what has to be supplied alongside it.

answer.exemplar: A mass spectrum reports the masses of the fragments a molecule breaks into, and many different structures share both a molecular formula and a set of fragment masses, so the spectrum constrains the formula without fixing the connectivity. The molecular ion pins the molar mass, which with nitrogen and oxygen rules narrows the elemental formula, but it says nothing about which groups were joined in which order, and isomers are indistinguishable to it. Infrared closes part of the gap by identifying functional groups through characteristic stretching and bending vibrations, and nuclear magnetic resonance closes more by counting distinct proton and carbon environments and showing through splitting and integration how those environments are connected. Each technique is blind to what the others see, which is exactly why structure assignment is described by what the combination of spectra rules out.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a blank must follow the same procedure
questions.learningObjective: justify running a blank through the identical procedure
questions.stem: Explain why a blank intended for a spectrophotometric determination has to be put through the identical procedure as the samples, with only the analyte omitted.

answer.exemplar: A blank works only if what it measures is exactly what is contaminating the samples, so every step that could contribute to the final reading has to be reproduced in it: the same solvent, the same buffer at the same pH, the same reagents from the same bottles, the same glassware with the same cleaning history, the same reaction time, and the same cell. Change one of those and the number being subtracted no longer matches the number that needs subtracting, so the correction is worse than none at all, because it also destroys the precision of the reading it was meant to protect. This is why a method blank and a reagent blank are reported separately: the first catches contamination introduced by handling, the second by the reagents themselves, and together they let an analyst say where the background came from rather than only that something was there. A blank also doubles as a check on the method, since a blank that should be clear but is not is the first sign that a reagent has gone off.

questions.learningObjective: state what a potentiometric titration measures as titrant is added

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state the assumption on which a gravimetric result rests
questions.stem: A gravimetric analysis precipitates a compound, weighs it, and computes the analyte from that mass. What assumption does the result rest on?

options.text: the isolated solid is pure, dry and of known composition, so its mass fixes the analyte mass
the precipitate is soluble, so it can be filtered off and then weighed after drying
options.misconception: believes a precipitate must dissolve to be weighed

options.text: the analyte is volatile, so it leaves the solution as the solid forms
options.misconception: treats a precipitate as material removed by evaporation

options.text: the weighing is done in solution, so the balance reads the concentration directly
options.misconception: believes the mass is measured on the liquid

questions.explanation: A gravimetric method converts the analyte into a solid compound of fixed composition, so the only route from a measured mass to an amount of analyte is the composition of that solid, and every impurity in it becomes an error in the result. That is why the precipitate is aged to grow large crystals, washed to remove adhering solution, and dried or ignited to a constant mass, so that the last step removes water and any volatile impurity. A precipitate that is fine, or that passes through the filter, or that is weighed wet, is the usual cause of a gravimetric result that runs high.
questions.hint: The measurement is a mass, so every gram of it must be attributable to the analyte.

questions.topic: Why a detector records against time

questions.stem: A detector in a chromatograph turns each eluting species into an electrical signal. Why is that signal recorded as a function of time rather than as a single total?

the total absorbed signal cannot be measured at all by a flow detector

options.misconception: overstates what a retention time proves about identity

questions.learningObjective: diagnose a systematic high bias from pipetting technique
questions.stem: A student uses a 25.00 mL volumetric pipette, drains the tip, then blows the liquid left in the stem into the receiving flask. Every titre from this pipette runs high. What is the flaw?

the pipette must be rinsed with the solution after calibration to displace the residual
options.misconception: believes rinsing after calibration corrects the delivered volume

options.text: the receiving flask should be rinsed with titrant so the measured volume is complete

options.text: the pipette should be held above the mark so the residual replaces what stayed behind

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a calibration needs several standards
questions.learningObjective: justify building a calibration from several standards
questions.stem: Explain why a calibration curve is built from several standards spanning a range of concentrations instead of a single standard.

answer.exemplar: One standard fixes a single point, and a single point cannot distinguish three different things that all matter: whether the response is proportional to concentration at all, what the response is when the analyte is absent, and how much the response drifts. With several standards spanning the working range the analyst can see the intercept, which is the cell and reagent background, and can test whether the points fall on a straight line, because a curve that bends is telling you the method has been pushed past the range where the response is proportional. The slope then converts any signal in between the standards into a concentration by interpolation, which is only defensible because bracketing standards exist on both sides of the unknown. A further reason is stability: repeating a calibration over a run reveals drift in lamp output or reagent composition, so the standards are doing double duty as a check on the instrument. The number of standards is a balance, since each one costs time but each one narrows the uncertainty in the fitted slope and lengthens the range that can be reported.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a titration curve jumps near equivalence
questions.learningObjective: explain the shape of a titration curve near equivalence
questions.stem: Explain why a titration curve changes so steeply in the region of the equivalence point, and how that shape affects how accurately an end point can be judged.

answer.exemplar: Away from the equivalence point the added titrant is being consumed by whatever is in excess, so its effect on the composition is small and the curve is nearly flat, and the flatness is what makes the position of equivalence unimportant there. Near the equivalence point the two species are almost balanced, and there a tiny addition of titrant converts a large fraction of what is left, because almost nothing is left to absorb it. The pH therefore swings through many units over a drop or two of titrant, and this steep section is where any detection method earns its accuracy. An indicator with a transition range inside that steep section gives an end point very close to equivalence, whereas one whose range falls on a flat part of the curve gives a badly placed end point no matter how carefully the colour is judged. It follows that a steeper curve permits a more dilute titration and a smaller sample, and that a weak acid titrated with a strong base gives a smaller jump than a strong acid does, which is why the choice of indicator depends on the pair being titrated.
